questions.q: Pooja writes the SI unit of force in her science notebook. Which way of writing the unit and its symbol is correct?
questions.a: newton, with the symbol N
o: newton, with the symbol N
Newton (capital N), with the symbol n
newton, with the symbol Nt
kilogram, with the symbol kg

questions.q: A gardener in Ooty ties a rope to a heavy flower pot and drags it across the lawn towards himself. What kind of force does he apply on the pot?
questions.a: A pull, as the rope draws the pot towards him
o: A pull, as the rope draws the pot towards him
A push, because the pot slides along the lawn as it moves
No force, because his hands never touch the pot itself
A push, because the rope presses against the side of the pot

questions.q:
Match each way of moving a box in Column I with the example in Column II.
Column I: 1. Pushing 2. Pulling 3. Lifting (pulling up) 4. Carrying
Column II: A. A porter walks along a railway platform with a suitcase on his head. B. A child drags a toy cart behind her by its string. C. A shopkeeper raises the rolling shutter of his shop from the ground. D. Two friends shove a stalled scooter from behind.

Assertion (A): As soon as Neha lets go of the door handle she was pulling, she stops feeling the handle pull on her hand.
Reason (R): An object that is at rest can still have forces acting on it.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Define force as the chapter does, and give one example of a force being applied in your classroom.
questions.a: A force is a push or pull on an object resulting from the object's interaction with another object. Example: pushing a desk across the floor, or pulling open the classroom door.
s: States that a force is a push or pull on an object resulting from its interaction with another object
Gives a correct classroom example, such as pushing a desk or pulling open a door

questions.q: Gaurav stretches a spring exerciser by pulling its two handles apart, one handle in each hand. (a) Which objects interact with the spring here, and is each applying a push or a pull on it? (b) Gaurav suddenly lets go of the right handle. What happens to the force on his right hand, and why?
questions.a: (a) His two hands interact with the spring through the handles; each hand pulls on the spring, and the spring pulls back on each hand. (b) The force on his right hand disappears at once, because that hand is no longer interacting with the spring; when an interaction ceases, the objects no longer experience the force.
s: (a) Names his two hands as the interacting objects, each applying a pull
(b) Says the force on the right hand disappears because the interaction has ended

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What is meant by a force in science? (b) What is the SI unit of force, and what is its symbol? (c) What is the least number of objects that must interact for a force to come into play?
questions.a: (a) A push or a pull applied on an object. (b) The newton; its symbol is N. (c) Two objects.
s: (a) A push or a pull applied on an object
(b) The newton, symbol N
(c) At least two objects

questions.q: Kabir pushes hard against his father's parked car, but the car does not move at all. He says, 'Since the car did not move, I applied no force on it, and it applied no force on me.' Check his claim. (a) Did Kabir apply a force on the car? Give a reason from the meaning of force. (b) Did the car apply a force on Kabir? How could he tell? (c) The car stayed at rest. What does the chapter say about the forces on an object that stays at rest?
questions.a: (a) Yes. A force is a push or pull on an object from its interaction with another object; Kabir's hands pushed the car whether or not it moved. (b) Yes. Whenever two objects interact, each experiences a force from the other, so Kabir would feel the car pressing back on his hands. (c) An object at rest can still have forces acting on it; it means the forces on it are balancing one another, not that there is no force. So Kabir's claim is wrong on both counts.
s: (a) Says yes, because pushing on the car is a force even without motion
(b) Says yes, each interacting object feels a force, felt as the car pressing back on his hands
(c) States that the forces on an object at rest balance one another, so the claim is wrong

questions.q:
Before the exams, four helpers at a school in Jabalpur shift furniture. Helper P pushes a desk across the floor with both hands. Helper Q ties a rope to a steel cupboard and drags it along the corridor; a force meter fixed in the rope reads 180 N. Helper R lifts a carton of answer sheets off the floor and carries it up the stairs. Helper S presses his palm hard against a wall for a whole minute, and the wall does not move.
(a) Which helper pushes an object and makes it move?
(b) Is Q's force on the cupboard a push or a pull, and what does the N in 180 N stand for?
(c) Name the two ways of moving the carton that R uses, in the words of the chapter.
(d) S says he applied no force because the wall did not move. Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Helper P. (b) A pull, applied through the rope; N stands for newton, the SI unit of force. (c) Lifting (pulling up) and carrying. (d) No. S pushes on the wall and the wall pushes back on his palm; a force comes from the interaction of two objects, and it acts even when nothing moves.
s: (a) Names Helper P
(b) Says pull, and that N stands for newton, the unit of force
(c) Lifting (pulling up) and carrying
(d) Says S is wrong, because his palm and the wall interact and push on each other even without motion

questions.q: Your teacher gives you only a rubber ball and a classroom wall. Plan a short demonstration, in steps, that shows three ideas: (i) a force is a push or a pull, (ii) a force needs at least two objects to interact, and (iii) each interacting object feels a force, and this force ends when the interaction ends. For each step, say what you do and what the class should notice.
questions.a: Step 1: Push the ball along the floor, then pull it back towards you by hooking your fingers behind it; the class sees that a force is a push or a pull. Step 2: Point out the two objects in each case, your hand and the ball; nothing happens to the ball until something interacts with it. Step 3: Press the ball against the wall with your palm; you feel the ball pressing back on your palm, so each object feels a force. Step 4: Take your hand away; the push on your palm stops at once, showing the force ends when the interaction ends.
s: A step that shows a push and a pull on the ball
Names the two interacting objects (hand and ball, or ball and wall) in the steps
A step where the palm presses the ball on the wall and feels the ball pressing back
A step showing the force on the hand ends the moment the hand is taken away

questions.q: Tara stamps on an empty juice carton lying on the floor, and the carton becomes flat. Which effect of force does this show?
questions.a: A change in the shape of the carton
o: A change in the shape of the carton
A change in the direction of motion of the carton
Making the carton move from rest
A change in the speed of the moving carton

questions.q: A football is flying straight towards the goal. The goalkeeper punches it, and it goes off sideways over the side line at about the same speed. Which effect of force does the punch show?
questions.a: A change in its direction of motion
o: A change in its direction of motion
Making it move from rest
A change in its shape only
No effect at all, as it was already moving

questions.q: In which of these events does a single touch change BOTH the speed and the direction of motion of a ball?
questions.a: A hockey player deflects a fast ball, and it moves off more slowly in a new direction
o: A hockey player deflects a fast ball, and it moves off more slowly in a new direction
A child gives a push to a ball lying still on the floor, and it rolls away across the whole room
A girl squeezes a soft ball that she is holding still in her fist until it is squashed flat
A boy presses down on a ball rolling straight ahead, and it slows down but keeps to the same line

questions.q:
Read three statements about what a force can do.
Statement I: A force can make an object at rest start moving.
Statement II: A force can change the shape of an object.
Statement III: A force can change the speed of a moving object, but never its direction.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: State any two effects that a force can have on an object, and give one everyday example of each.
questions.a: Any two, each with an example: it can make an object move from rest (kicking a football lying still); change the speed of a moving object (applying brakes on a moving bicycle); change its direction of motion (turning the handle of a moving bicycle); change its shape (stretching a rubber band).
s: States one effect of force with a matching example
States a second, different effect with a matching example

questions.q: True or false? Give a reason. 'When Ravi steps on a soft rubber ball rolling towards him, the push from his foot can only stop the ball; it cannot also change the ball's shape at the same moment.'
questions.a: False. A force can cause some or all of its effects together. Ravi's push stops the ball, which is a change in its speed, and at the same time presses the soft ball out of shape.
s: States False
Explains that a force can cause some or all of its effects together, so the push can stop the ball and change its shape

questions.q: Name the effect of force in each action. (a) Applying the brakes of a moving scooter. (b) Pulling a rubber band to stretch it. (c) Turning the handle of a moving bicycle at a corner.
questions.a: (a) It decreases the speed of the scooter and can stop it. (b) It changes the shape of the rubber band. (c) It changes the direction of motion of the bicycle.
s: (a) Change (decrease) in speed
(b) Change in shape
(c) Change in direction of motion

questions.q: Diya says, 'Whenever a moving object changes its direction, a force must be acting on it. But an object can change its shape without any force at all.' (a) Is the first part of her claim right? Give a reason. (b) Is the second part right? Give a reason. (c) Give one everyday example that tests the second part.
questions.a: Her claim is only partly right. (a) Yes. A change in the direction of motion does not happen without a force acting. (b) No. A change in shape is also an effect of force; none of the changes in speed, direction or shape takes place without the action of a force. (c) A rubber band changes shape only when it is pulled; a chapati is flattened only when the rolling pin presses on it.
s: (a) Agrees with the first part: a change in direction needs a force
(b) Rejects the second part: a change in shape is also an effect of force
(c) Gives an example where the shape changes only when a force is applied

questions.q:
In a football drill at a school in Guwahati, a coach films one ball through four touches. Touch 1: the ball lies still; Riya kicks it and it rolls north at 6 m/s. Touch 2: Tanvi taps it from behind, and it keeps rolling north at 9 m/s. Touch 3: Aman nudges it from the side, and it now rolls east, still at 9 m/s. Touch 4: Kiran stamps on it; it stops dead and is squashed flat for a moment.
(a) Which effect of force did Touch 1 produce?
(b) What did Touch 2 change, and by how much?
(c) In Touch 3, what changed and what stayed the same?
(d) The coach gives a badge to the player whose single touch produced more than one effect of force. Who should get it? Justify.
questions.a: (a) It made the ball move from rest. (b) It changed the speed of the ball, increasing it by 9 - 6 = 3 m/s. (c) The direction of motion changed from north to east; the speed stayed the same at 9 m/s. (d) Kiran. Her touch changed the speed (from 9 m/s to 0, stopping the ball) and also changed its shape. Each of the other touches produced only one effect.
s: (a) Made the ball move from rest
(b) Increased the speed by 3 m/s
(c) Direction changed from north to east, speed stayed 9 m/s
(d) Chooses Kiran, because her touch changed both speed and shape while the others changed one thing each

questions.q:
For each action, say whether a push or a pull is applied on the object in brackets, and name the main effect of the force on it.
(a) A coolie drags a trolley bag that was standing still on the platform [bag].
(b) A girl squeezes half a lemon over her dal [lemon].
(c) A policeman grabs the handle of a runaway handcart and holds it back until it stops [handcart].
(d) A player heads a football flying towards him back the way it came [football].
(e) A shopkeeper pulls open a closed sliding glass door [door].
questions.a: (a) Pull; it makes the bag move from rest. (b) Push (squeeze); it changes the shape of the lemon. (c) Pull; it decreases the speed of the handcart and stops it. (d) Push; it changes the direction of motion of the football. (e) Pull; it makes the door move from rest.
s: (a) Pull, makes the bag move from rest
(b) Push, changes the shape of the lemon
(c) Pull, decreases the speed and stops the handcart
(d) Push, changes the direction of motion of the football
(e) Pull, makes the door move from rest

questions.q: A notebook is given a push and slides towards the east along a bench. In which direction does friction act on the notebook while it slides?
questions.a: Towards the west, opposite to its motion
o: Towards the west, opposite to its motion
Towards the east, along its motion
Straight upward, away from the bench
In no direction, as it is already slowing

questions.q: Racing swimmers wear tight, smooth caps that give the head a rounded, streamlined shape. Which idea from the chapter best explains this choice?
questions.a: Water exerts friction on a moving object, and a special shape reduces it
o: Water exerts friction on a moving object, and a special shape reduces it
Friction acts only between solid surfaces, so the cap only keeps the hair dry
A smooth cap increases the friction from the water, so the swimmer grips it
The cap reduces the gravitational force of the Earth acting on the swimmer's body

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Given the same push, a steel tiffin box slides further on a glass table top than on a jute mat.
Reason (R): Friction is greater on smoother surfaces.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the force in Column II.
Column I: 1. A pair of bullocks pulling a loaded cart 2. A carrom coin slowing down on the board 3. An aeroplane given a special shape 4. The heart making blood circulate
Column II: A. Muscular force inside the body B. Friction between two solid surfaces C. Muscular force of animals used for human tasks D. Friction due to the air
What are contact forces? Name the two contact forces described in this chapter.
questions.a: Contact forces are forces that act only when there is physical contact between the objects, either directly (with hands or other body parts) or indirectly (through a stick or rope). The two described are muscular force and friction.
s: States that contact forces act only when the objects are in physical contact, directly or through a stick or rope
Names muscular force and friction

questions.q: True or false? Give a reason. 'Friction acts on an object only after it has started moving, and not while it is merely trying to move.'
questions.a: False. Friction comes into play when an object moves or tries to move over another surface, and it acts opposite to the direction in which the object is moving or trying to move.
s: States False
Explains that friction acts when an object moves or tries to move over a surface

questions.q: Write one everyday situation for each of the following. (a) Muscular force at work inside your own body. (b) Friction making a moving object stop sooner on a rough surface than on a smooth one. (c) Friction from air or water acting on a moving vehicle, and how its effect is reduced.
questions.a: Sample answers: (a) The muscles of the jaw help us chew food, or the heart muscles expand and contract to circulate blood. (b) A bicycle that stops being pedalled stops sooner on a rough village road than on a smooth tar road. (c) A boat moving through a lake faces friction from the water, so boats are built with a special shape to reduce it.
s: (a) A correct use of muscular force inside the body, such as chewing, moving food along the alimentary canal or the heartbeat
(b) A correct situation where a moving object stops sooner on the rougher surface
(c) A vehicle moving through air or water, with special shaping named as the way to reduce friction

questions.q:
A cycling club in Pune tests helmets for a 40 km race. Each helmet is moved through the air at racing speed, and a force meter shows the force of friction from the air on it: round helmet 12 N, round helmet with a loose cloth cover 14 N, long helmet with a pointed tail 7 N. A pointed helmet costs ₹4,500 and a round helmet ₹1,200. The riders turn the pedals with their leg muscles.
(a) Which force do the riders use to turn the pedals, and is it a contact or a non-contact force?
(b) In which direction does the friction from the air act on a moving rider?
(c) By how many newtons does the pointed helmet reduce the friction compared with the plain round helmet?
(d) The club has ₹12,000 to buy helmets for its 4 racers. Can it give all four the pointed helmet? What is the best it can do, and should anyone use the cloth cover?
questions.a: (a) Muscular force; it is a contact force, because the feet are in contact with the pedals. (b) Opposite to the direction in which the rider is moving. (c) 12 - 7 = 5 N less. (d) No: 4 x ₹4,500 = ₹18,000, which is more than ₹12,000. Three pointed and one round cost ₹14,700, still too much, so the best is 2 pointed and 2 round helmets for ₹11,400. No one should use the cloth cover, because it raises the friction from 12 N to 14 N.
s: (a) Muscular force, a contact force
(b) Opposite to the direction of motion
(c) 5 N less
(d) Shows ₹18,000 is over budget, chooses 2 pointed and 2 round (₹11,400), and rejects the cloth cover because it adds friction

questions.q:
A class 'myth-buster' board has five claims about contact forces. For each, say whether it is right or wrong, and give the reason from the chapter.
(a) 'A horse pulling a tonga uses a non-contact force, because the horse never touches the tonga itself.'
(b) 'Muscular force helps push food along the alimentary canal.'
(c) 'A highly polished marble floor has no irregularities at all, so there is no friction on it.'
(d) 'A fish swimming through a river has to move against friction from the water.'
(e) 'If a box is pushed towards the left, friction on it acts towards the left as well.'
questions.a: (a) Wrong. Contact can be indirect, through ropes or poles; the horse's muscular force is a contact force. (b) Right. Muscular force helps us chew food and push it through the alimentary canal. (c) Wrong. Even surfaces that look smooth have many minute irregularities, so there is still some friction, only less than on a rough surface. (d) Right. Water and other liquids exert friction on objects moving through them. (e) Wrong. Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, so it acts towards the right.
s: (a) Wrong, because indirect contact through ropes or poles is still contact
(b) Right, muscular force moves food along the alimentary canal
(c) Wrong, smooth-looking surfaces still have minute irregularities and some friction
(d) Right, water exerts friction on objects moving through it
(e) Wrong, friction acts opposite to the motion, towards the right

questions.q: Jose rows a small boat across the backwaters near Kollam by pulling the oars with his arms. (a) Which force does Jose use to pull the oars? (b) Is this a contact force or a non-contact force? Give a reason. (c) When he stops rowing, the boat slowly comes to a stop. Name the force from the water that slows it down. (d) Why are boats and ships built with special shapes?
questions.a: (a) Muscular force. (b) A contact force, because his hands are in physical contact with the oars. (c) Friction exerted by the water. (d) To reduce the force of friction due to the water around them.
s: (a) Muscular force
(b) Contact force, because his hands touch the oars
(c) Friction from the water
(d) To reduce the friction due to the water

questions.q: Two bar magnets are brought close to each other. Which pair of poles will attract each other?
questions.a: A North pole and a South pole
o: A North pole and a South pole
A North pole and a North pole
A South pole and a South pole
Any two poles, whichever face each other

questions.q: Balloon P has just been rubbed with a woollen cloth. A plastic straw Y hanging nearby swings away from balloon P without being touched. What can you conclude about straw Y?
questions.a: It is charged, with the same kind of charge as balloon P
o: It is charged, with the same kind of charge as balloon P
It is uncharged, since charged objects push uncharged objects away
It is charged, with the opposite kind of charge to balloon P
It must be a magnet, since only magnets push from a distance

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A balloon rubbed with a woollen cloth is attracted by that same cloth.
Reason (R): The rubbing object and the rubbed object get opposite kinds of charge, and unlike charges attract each other.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement I: Static charges are given this name because they move about freely by themselves.
Statement II: A charged object can attract small uncharged pieces of paper without touching them.
Statement III: Magnetic force and electrostatic force can each be either attractive or repulsive.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III

questions.q: (a) What is electrostatic force? (b) Is it a contact force or a non-contact force?
questions.a: (a) The force exerted by a charged body on another charged body or on an uncharged body. (b) It is a non-contact force.
s: (a) Defines it as the force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body
(b) States that it is a non-contact force

questions.q: Two identical plastic straws are each rubbed with the same piece of polythene and hung near each other. They move apart. (a) Why do the straws move apart? (b) Predict what happens when the piece of polythene is brought near one of the straws, and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Both straws were charged in the same way, so they carry like (similar) charges, and like charges repel. (b) The straw and the polythene move towards each other, because the rubbing object and the rubbed object get opposite (unlike) kinds of charge, and unlike charges attract.
s: (a) The straws carry like charges, and like charges repel
(b) Predicts attraction, because the polythene and the straw carry unlike charges

questions.q: (a) What is magnetic force? (b) What do the like poles of two magnets do to each other? (c) Why is magnetic force called a non-contact force?
questions.a: (a) The force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or on a magnetic material. (b) Like poles repel each other. (c) Because a magnet can exert this force from a distance, without being in contact with the other object.
s: (a) Force exerted by a magnet on another magnet or a magnetic material
(b) Like poles repel
(c) It acts from a distance without contact

questions.q: A science-fair card says: 'Object P pushed object Q away from a distance of 3 cm, and nobody touched either of them.' (a) Show that this push cannot be due to the Earth's gravitational force. (b) Show that it cannot be muscular force or friction. (c) Name the two forces from the chapter that could explain it, and say what arrangement of each would give a push.
questions.a: (a) Gravitational force is always attractive and never repulsive, so it cannot push Q away. (b) Muscular force and friction are contact forces that act only when objects are in contact, but P and Q were not touching. (c) Magnetic force, if like poles of two magnets face each other, or electrostatic force, if P and Q carry like charges; in both cases like ones repel.
s: (a) Gravity is always attractive, so it cannot push
(b) Muscular force and friction need contact, and there was none
(c) Names magnetic force (like poles) and electrostatic force (like charges)

questions.q:
On a dry winter day in Shimla, Class 8 students hang two balloons, A and B, on threads so that they hang 10 cm apart. They rub both balloons with the same woollen scarf and let go; the balloons swing away from each other until they are 18 cm apart. When the scarf is brought near balloon A, A swings towards it. Held 4 cm above some tiny bits of paper on the desk, balloon A makes the bits jump up and stick to it.
(a) Name the force that pushed the balloons apart.
(b) Do A and B carry like or unlike charges? Give a reason.
(c) Why does balloon A swing towards the scarf?
(d) Tenzin says the balloons have become magnets, because they pull and push without touching. Is he right? Use the rubbing and the paper bits to decide.
questions.a: (a) Electrostatic force, a non-contact force. (b) Like charges: both were charged in the same way, by the same scarf, and they repelled each other, and like charges repel. (c) The scarf, the rubbing object, got the opposite kind of charge to the balloon, and unlike charges attract. (d) No. The balloons got static charges by rubbing; a charged object attracts small uncharged pieces of paper, while a magnet attracts only magnets and magnetic materials, which paper is not. Pulling and pushing without contact happens with both forces, so it does not prove they are magnets.
s: (a) Electrostatic force
(b) Like charges, because they were charged the same way and repelled
(c) The scarf carries the opposite charge, and unlike charges attract
(d) Says Tenzin is wrong: the balloons were charged by rubbing and attract paper, which a magnet would not; non-contact action alone does not prove magnetism

questions.q:
A teacher puts these on a tray: two bar magnets with marked poles, an iron nail, a plastic scale freshly rubbed with polythene, the piece of polythene used to rub it, and tiny bits of paper. For each pair below, say whether the two attract or repel each other, and name the force.
(a) The North pole of one magnet and the iron nail.
(b) The North pole of one magnet and the North pole of the other.
(c) The North pole of one magnet and the South pole of the other.
(d) The rubbed scale and the bits of paper.
(e) The rubbed scale and the piece of polythene.
questions.a: (a) Attract; magnetic force, since iron is a magnetic material. (b) Repel; magnetic force, since like poles repel. (c) Attract; magnetic force, since unlike poles attract. (d) Attract; electrostatic force, since a charged object attracts small uncharged pieces of paper. (e) Attract; electrostatic force, since the rubbing and rubbed objects get opposite charges, and unlike charges attract.
s: (a) Attract, magnetic force
(b) Repel, magnetic force
(c) Attract, magnetic force
(d) Attract, electrostatic force
(e) Attract, electrostatic force, because they carry opposite charges

questions.q: Which statement about the Earth's gravitational force is correct?
questions.a: It is always an attractive force
o: It is always an attractive force
It can attract or repel, like magnetic force
It acts only on objects touching the ground
It acts only on objects that are falling

questions.q: A spring balance in a school lab has 4 equal small divisions between its 0 N mark and its 1 N mark. What is the smallest weight it can read?
o: 4 N

questions.q: Shruti throws a ball straight up. At its highest point, the ball stops for an instant before it starts to fall. Which force acts on the ball at that instant?
questions.a: The Earth's gravitational force, pulling it downward
o: The Earth's gravitational force, pulling it downward
No force at all, because the ball has stopped moving
The Earth's gravitational force, pushing it upward
Only the upward force left over from Shruti's hand

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A stone dropped from a rooftop falls along a straight vertical path to the ground.
Reason (R): The weight of an object can change from place to place, though its mass does not.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or false? Give a reason. 'A packet of rice with a mass of 2 kg on the Earth still has a mass of 2 kg on the Moon.'
questions.a: True. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and its value remains the same at every place; only the weight, the pull of gravity on it, changes.
s: States True
Explains that mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere, while weight changes

questions.q: On the Earth a 1 kg mass weighs about 10 N, and on Mars it weighs 3.8 N. Take the weight to be in proportion to the mass. (a) Find the weight on the Earth of a bag of potatoes of mass 4 kg. (b) Find the weight of the same bag on Mars.
questions.a: (a) 4 x 10 N = 40 N. (b) 4 x 3.8 N = 15.2 N; its mass is still 4 kg.
s: (a) 40 N on the Earth
(b) 15.2 N on Mars

questions.q: A spring balance has a range of 0 to 5 N, and there are 10 equal small divisions between each pair of 1 N marks. (a) What is the smallest weight it can read? (b) The pointer stops 3 small divisions after the 2 N mark. What is the reading? (c) On the Earth a 1 kg mass weighs about 10 N. Should this balance be used to weigh a bag of mass 2 kg? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 1 N / 10 = 0.1 N. (b) 2 N + 3 x 0.1 N = 2.3 N. (c) No. The bag weighs about 2 x 10 = 20 N, which is more than the 5 N the balance can measure, so the balance may get damaged.
s: (c) No, because about 20 N is more than the 5 N maximum and may damage the balance

questions.q:
At a space exhibition in Sriharikota, a stall displays a pack of mass 1 kg with a chart of its weight on five bodies: Earth 10 N, Moon 1.6 N, Mars 3.8 N, Venus 9 N and Jupiter 25.4 N. Visitors can hang the pack from a spring balance in a simulator that copies the pull on each body.
(a) On which body does the pack weigh the least?
(b) What is the mass of the pack on Jupiter?
(c) How many newtons more does the pack weigh on the Earth than on Mars?
(d) In which simulator would the spring of the balance stretch the most? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The Moon (1.6 N). (b) 1 kg; mass stays the same everywhere. (c) 10 - 3.8 = 6.2 N more. (d) The Jupiter simulator, because the pull on the pack (its weight, 25.4 N) is greatest there, and a greater weight stretches the spring more.
s: (a) The Moon
(b) 1 kg, since mass does not change
(d) Jupiter, because the weight (pull) is greatest there and stretches the spring most

questions.q: A school lab has three spring balances. Balance A reads 0 to 10 N, with 5 equal small divisions between each pair of 1 N marks. Balance B reads 0 to 2.5 N, with big marks every 0.5 N and 10 equal small divisions between them. Balance C reads 0 to 50 N, with big marks every 5 N and 2 equal small divisions between them. Ananya must weigh a key ring of weight 0.35 N, a water bottle of weight 8 N and a school bag of weight 30 N, each as exactly as possible, without damaging any balance. Find the smallest reading of each balance, and decide which balance she should use for each object. Justify your choices.
questions.a: Smallest readings: A = 1 N / 5 = 0.2 N, B = 0.5 N / 10 = 0.05 N, C = 5 N / 2 = 2.5 N. An object must not be heavier than the balance's maximum, so B (2.5 N) cannot take the bottle or the bag, and A (10 N) cannot take the bag. Key ring: only B can show 0.35 N exactly (7 small divisions); A could show only 0.2 N or 0.4 N. Water bottle: A shows 8 N exactly, while C can show only 7.5 N or 10 N, so use A. School bag: only C can take 30 N, and it shows it exactly (12 small divisions). So B for the key ring, A for the bottle and C for the bag.
s: Finds the smallest readings 0.2 N, 0.05 N and 2.5 N
Rules out any balance whose maximum is less than the object's weight
Chooses B for the key ring, A for the bottle and C for the bag
Justifies with the smallest readings: only B shows 0.35 N, and A shows 8 N exactly while C cannot

questions.q: Compare the Earth's gravitational force with magnetic force under these four headings, giving the fact from the chapter for each: (a) whether it is a contact or a non-contact force, (b) whether it can only attract, or can attract and also repel, (c) which objects it acts on, (d) one everyday example of each.
questions.a: (a) Both are non-contact forces; they act without touching. (b) Gravitational force is always attractive; magnetic force can attract (unlike poles) or repel (like poles). (c) The Earth's gravity pulls all objects towards it, since every object thrown up comes back down; magnetic force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. (d) Gravitational: a fruit falling from a tree. Magnetic: a magnet pulling an iron nail, or a compass needle pointing North.
s: (a) Both are non-contact forces
(b) Gravity always attracts; magnetic force can attract or repel
(c) Gravity acts on all objects; magnetic force acts on magnets and magnetic materials
(d) A correct example of each

questions.q: Arjun pushes a beach ball down into a swimming pool and feels it pushing up against his hands. What is this upward force from the water called?
questions.a: Upthrust, or buoyant force
o: Upthrust, or buoyant force
The gravitational force on the ball
Friction exerted by the water
Electrostatic force

questions.q: A wooden block weighing 6 N floats in a tank of water. Mohan pushes it further down with his finger and holds it there, so that it now pushes aside water weighing 9 N. While he holds it there, what is the buoyant force on the block?
questions.a: 9 N
o: 9 N
6 N
3 N

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement I: All liquids, not only water, apply an upward force on objects placed in them.
Statement II: The buoyant force on an object in water acts downward, in the same direction as gravity.
Statement III: An object floats when the buoyant force on it is equal to the gravitational force on it.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Upthrust 2. Archimedes' Principle 3. Pumice 4. A mug of water still inside a bucket of water
Column II: A. A light, porous rock full of air pockets that floats on water B. Feels lighter than after it is lifted out C. The upward force a liquid applies on an object in it D. The upward force on an immersed object equals the weight of the liquid it displaces
True or false? Give a reason. 'A stone lying at the bottom of a pond still has a buoyant force acting on it.'
questions.a: True. Any object fully or partly immersed in a liquid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces. The stone sinks because this force is smaller than its weight, not because the force is zero.
s: States True
Explains that the immersed stone gets an upward force equal to the weight of water it displaces, which is less than its weight

questions.q: State Archimedes' Principle, and use it to say when an object will sink in a liquid.
questions.a: When an object is fully or partially immersed in a liquid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces. The object sinks if the weight of the liquid it displaces is smaller than its own weight.
s: States that an immersed object experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces
Says the object sinks if the weight of liquid displaced is smaller than the object's weight

questions.q: An empty plastic jerrycan with its cap tightly closed is pushed down into a village water tank and then let go. (a) What do you feel on your hands as you push it down? (b) What does the jerrycan do when it is let go? (c) In which direction does the Earth's gravitational force act on the jerrycan while it is in the water?
questions.a: (a) An upward push from the water, the buoyant force (upthrust). (b) It bounces back up to the surface of the water. (c) Downward.
s: (a) An upward push (buoyant force) from the water
(b) It bounces back up to the surface
(c) Downward

questions.q: Lata says, 'The buoyant force on an object depends only on how heavy the object is, so two objects of the same weight always get the same buoyant force.' In a test, a stone weighing 10 N, held fully under water, displaces water weighing 4 N, while a wooden log weighing 10 N floats, displacing water weighing 10 N. (a) Find the buoyant force on each object. (b) Does the data support Lata's claim? (c) What does the buoyant force actually equal, according to Archimedes' Principle?
questions.a: (a) Stone: 4 N; log: 10 N. (b) No. Both weigh 10 N, but their buoyant forces are 4 N and 10 N, so equal weights do not give equal buoyant forces. (c) It equals the weight of the liquid the object displaces.
s: (a) 4 N on the stone and 10 N on the log
(b) Rejects the claim, since the same weight gave different buoyant forces
(c) The weight of the liquid displaced

questions.q:
A geology club in Port Blair collects three stones from a beach near a volcano. They weigh each stone, then hold it fully under water and find the weight of water it pushes aside. Stone P (pumice) weighs 0.6 N and displaces 0.9 N. Stone Q (pumice) weighs 1.0 N and displaces 1.1 N. Stone R (basalt) weighs 2.7 N and displaces 0.9 N. Rule: a stone floats if, when held fully under, the water it pushes aside weighs at least as much as the stone (with anything it carries); otherwise it sinks.
(a) Which stone will sink?
(b) What is the buoyant force on stone R while it is fully under water?
(c) Why is pumice light enough to float, according to how it forms?
(d) A craft shop wants a floating stone that can carry a tea-light weighing 0.2 N on top. Which stone or stones will work? Show the check.
questions.a: (a) Stone R, since 0.9 N is less than its weight of 2.7 N. (b) 0.9 N, the weight of the water it displaces. (c) Pumice forms when lava with lots of gas and water vapour cools quickly and traps tiny gas bubbles, giving a light, porous rock full of air pockets. (d) Only stone P: 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8 N, which is not more than 0.9 N, so it floats. Stone Q: 1.0 + 0.2 = 1.2 N, more than 1.1 N, so it sinks; stone R sinks anyway.
s: (a) Stone R
(c) Lava with gas cools quickly and traps bubbles, making a light rock with air pockets
(d) Checks 0.8 N against 0.9 N and 1.2 N against 1.1 N, and chooses stone P only

questions.q:
A ferry canoe at a ghat in Varanasi weighs 1,200 N. When it is loaded until the water reaches its top edge, it pushes aside water weighing 5,000 N; with any more load, water pours in. The boatman weighs 600 N and each passenger about 550 N.
(a) The empty canoe floats. What is the buoyant force on it?
(b) How much load (people) can the canoe carry before the water reaches its top edge?
(c) What would be the total weight of the canoe with the boatman and 6 passengers?
(d) With the boatman on board, how many passengers can it take at most?
(e) A board at the ghat says 'Not more than 6 passengers'. Should the boatman follow the board for this canoe? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 1,200 N; a floating object gets a buoyant force equal to its weight. (b) 5,000 - 1,200 = 3,800 N. (c) 1,200 + 600 + 6 x 550 = 5,100 N. (d) 3,800 - 600 = 3,200 N is left for passengers; 3,200 / 550 is about 5.8, so at most 5 passengers. (e) No. With 6 passengers the total, 5,100 N, is more than the 5,000 N of water the canoe can push aside, so water would pour in; for this canoe he should take at most 5.
s: (a) 1,200 N, equal to its weight as it floats
(b) 3,800 N of load
(d) At most 5 passengers
(e) Rejects the board's limit because 5,100 N is more than 5,000 N, and keeps to 5 passengers
